title: Chapter 47 – What It Costs
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

His mother comes through the seam with a knife in each hand and her hood thrown back, and the first thing she says is his name.

"Jian."

"I'm here."

"Are you hurt?"

"No."

"Are you lying?"

"No, Mother. Look."

She looks. She crosses the moss in six long strides, and her hands go over him in the quick rough way she has when she is afraid, over the shoulders, the ribs, the back of the neck, the face. He lets her. When she is quite sure, she goes on holding his arms a moment longer than she needs to. Her hands are cold and not entirely steady. He thinks she has not slept at all.

Behind her, the green seam hangs in the air, a vertical line, with a ragged glimmer of starlight showing through it from the other side. The note of the Bell is still fading in the high stone dark above them. It has been, by her account, a little under three hours. In the quarry the moon has set and the sky is turning gray.

"I heard a bell," says Qinghe. Her voice is level. "I heard it from the quarry, in the middle of the night, and the earth hummed. The pines hummed. I thought the whole hill was going to wake." She lets go of him and straightens. "And the air opened. And I thought, that is the door he promised me. And I came."

"I'm sorry."

"Do not be sorry. Be accurate." She lifts her head, and looks at the Orchard for the first time.

* * *

She does not speak for a long time.

She stands at the edge of the moss with her knives forgotten in her hands. The pale light drifts across her face. Her lips part. In the green haze, in the endless rows of tall dark plants, in the steaming gleam of the pool and the great glowing vault of the ceiling, she is a small gray figure, quite still, like someone who has walked through a door into a memory.

"There was a garden," she says, finally, in a strange voice. "On the river. When I was a girl. An old man kept it. He grew herbs for the boatmen. Willow bark, comfrey, a little poppy." A pause. "It smelled like this. When it had rained. I used to sit in it and pretend it was mine."

"Mother."

"I am all right." She shakes her head. "I am trying to understand what I am looking at. It is a hall. A hidden hall of medicine, under a hill that has been hungry for four hundred years." She turns, and her eyes are bright. "Wenyuan does not know."

"No."

"Nobody knows."

"Hu guessed there was a door. I think. He did not guess this."

She takes a long slow breath.

"Then we will have to decide," she says. "Very carefully. Who is to know." She puts her knives away, one by one, into her sleeves, and for the first time since the quarry the lines round her mouth ease. "But first you will tell me everything. As a clan asks."

He has been thinking about what to say for three hours. He tells her about the pangolin, and the seam, and Pebble's mother. He tells her about the Wardens, and the gardener. He tells her about the reservoir, and the heart plate, and the half scroll. He tells her that something small and gray, a thing that was given to him in a cave long ago, has sunk into his chest and is humming there now.

He does not tell her what it is. He tells her, truthfully, that he does not understand it.

She listens with her head bowed. When he has finished, she is silent a long time.

"A seed," she says at last. "For the five roots."

"For mine. I think."

"And only half."

"Yes."

"Then we shall have to be kind to your half." Her mouth moves in something that is not quite a smile. "And find the other."

* * *

Mei Ru is dying.

He has known it since the second hour, and has not said it. He has told himself the Warden's roots are healing her, that the Blood Seal worked, that she is young and strong. It is not true. The color has not come back to her lips. The rust-colored cloak lies over her like a leaf. When Qinghe kneels beside her, and lays two fingers against the thin neck, her face changes.

"She is cold."

"I know."

"It is the Blood Fox." Qinghe's voice is clipped. "It was meant to be the last act. She burned what her body could spare, and the rest went with it. Whatever the pill did, it bought her a day. Not more." She draws back. "I have seen it in river-men, after a long fever. They lie there, and they say they are fine, and then they are not."

The woman's eyes open.

They are very clear. They look first at Jian, then at Qinghe, and a thin dry amusement moves in them. "The mother," says Mei Ru, in a whisper. "I wondered. You were behind the wheel. Tally said a woman with two knives. Mei Lian was angry with you."

"I am sorry for your sister."

"No, you are not. But thank you for saying it." Her gaze goes back to the green stone sky. "How long have I?"

"I do not know," says Qinghe, honestly. "A day. Perhaps less."

"Good. I am so tired." She wets her lips. "I would like to tell you something. In exchange for a funeral. I would like to be burned with my sister. Her body is on the road to Three Willows, in a cart. Mu will have it burned in the Sect fashion, a drop of blood in the fire, and a bow." Her eyes close. "I do not wish to be bowed to."

"We will find her," says Jian.

He does not know why he says it. It is out before he thinks. Qinghe's eyes flick to him, and she says nothing.

"Mu is a patient man," says Mei Ru, to the ceiling. "I want you to understand that. He will not send another drummer. He will come himself. Within ten days. There is a window, an old woman who reads the hill, and he will want it, and he will not wait to be told it is safe." She swallows. "He has a master, in the Rill stage, dying. He needs a key for a door. A seamwalker, and a refiner's book. That is all I know. I have not been told where the door is. I have been told it is under something."

"Under what?"

"A pool." Her mouth moves. "Everything the Blood Shadow wants is always under a pool."

Pool, thinks Jian. He looks at the green water behind him, at the white rim of stone, and a cold finger runs down his back.

"He will bring three or four others," Mei Ru goes on, faintly. "Not Drips. Men from the Pool stage, who can walk in the sunlight without burning. A priest, perhaps. I do not know their names." A dry little laugh. "I do not know anything. I was a girl with a chain. It was enough. It was enough for a long time."

Her breathing slows. For a while nobody speaks. In the beds beyond the pool, a little silver-leafed plant turns its face toward the faint light of the stone, as it has been doing for four hundred years.

"Little boy," says Mei Ru.

"Yes."

"Why did you give me the pill?"

He thinks about it. He thinks about it honestly, with all the care he has. It is the only answer he owes.

"Because I did not want to be someone who would not," he says.

"Ah." It is almost a sigh. "That is not a reason. It is a... a vanity." She smiles. It is a small thing, and quite sweet, and not at all unkind. "I am glad. I am so glad. Mu would have been pleased by it. He likes a good vanity."

"Mei Ru?"

She does not answer.

It happens between one breath and the next. There is no sound. Her face, which has been tight with pain for a day and a night, simply loosens, like a hand letting go of a rope. The Warden's roots slacken, and fall, and sink away into the moss.

The amber lamp of the gate keeper dims, and goes out.

* * *

They burn her at dawn, on the hillside, in the cold, with no one but the two of them.

It is not an honor. It is the only thing Jian can think of. There is a hollow behind the quarry where the spoil has been dumped, and they build the pyre there out of dry pine and slag and a rotten beam, with Mei Ru wrapped in her rust-colored cloak. Qinghe lights it. She does it without ceremony, with a flint, and for a long time neither of them speaks.

The smoke goes up in a thin gray column. It is not white. It is not clean. It smells of old blood, and of the thing under it, the sweetness, the faint cold taste of lilies.

"I should not have promised," says Jian. "About the sister."

"No."

"I do not know how to find her."

"No." His mother is looking at the fire. "But you promised. And you meant it. That is not a small thing." A pause. "It will be harder to do than to say. It generally is."

"It was not true. What she said. About it being a vanity."

"It was a little true."

"Mother—"

"It is always a little true, Jian." She turns her head. In the gray morning she looks very tired, and very sure. "You are nineteen years old, and you are good with a needle, and you have spent two months killing people who came to hurt us. I have not stopped you. I am not going to. But you will go on finding, as the years go by, that the thing you have to defend is not only the clan. It is the part of you that gave a dying woman a pill." She picks up a stick and prods the fire. "That part is fragile. It is worth more than the hill."

He does not answer. In the smoke, very high, a small brown bird is circling.

"Now," says Qinghe. "Tell me what it costs."

* * *

What what costs?

"The thing," says his mother. "The Orchard. The pangolin. The seam. You have told me everything but that. Do not tell me there is no price. I have kept a household for twenty years, and I have never found a thing that was free."

He sits down on a stone. He had not meant to say it. He finds that he has been waiting to.

"Pebble," he says. "It's Pebble."

She is asleep in his lap. She has been sleeping since the Orchard, curled round on herself like a fiddlehead fern, with her tail over her nose. Her scales are dull. He can see the places where three of them have come loose, small pale scars along her side, like missing teeth.

"Every seam she opens costs her something," he says. "She does not say. I can feel it. In the Narrows, she lost one. In the quarry she lost another. Then the door in the hill, that was the third." He touches the scar with a finger. "They do not grow back quickly. She is not yet a year old. She is, I think, a good deal younger than a year, for a seamwalker. If she does it ten times, she'll be a naked thing."

"And then?"

"I don't know. Hu says that old seamwalkers do not use their gift at all. They keep it, like a coin. They use it once, at the end." He swallows. "Her mother used it once. For the bell. She went out and did not come back."

Qinghe says nothing.

"I will not ask her," Jian says. "Not again. Not unless I have to. And I think that is the first thing the Orchard costs. I think it costs a very small person a very great deal." He looks at the bird. "And she has not once refused me."

His mother's hand comes out, and rests on his head. She has not done that in a long time. It is warm, and light, and a little rough, and he finds he has to look away.

"And the second thing?" she says gently.

"The second is mine. But there is a third."

* * *

The third he learns on the way.

It is Limp that tells him, in its way, through Pebble. They are walking back along the herb beds, the pangolin awake on his shoulder and the small lame Warden creaking at his heel, when it stops at a bed of dying sunfern and lays one twig-hand on the soil.

It says the ground is thirsty, Pebble translates. It says the beds are drinking the hill.

"Drinking it how?"

From under. Through the roots. It says the pool is very small, and the Orchard is very old, and a long time ago it was fed by a great vein, a big one, and the vein was cut. A pause. It says the Orchard has been reaching up into the hill for four hundred years, to find more.

He stands very still.

The vein is three parts in a hundred, he thinks. He has read it in Wenyuan's ledger, in the long slow fall of the hill's yield, year on year. And in the last month it has fallen faster, because Pebble came near, and something under the hill began to wake.

It is not only that the vein is dying, he thinks. Something is taking it.

He looks at the dim green beds, and the little pool, and the Wardens standing in their ring, patient and faithful and dim, holding together a formation that has not had enough to eat for four centuries. He does not feel anger. He cannot find any. It is a garden, and it is hungry, and it has done what a hungry thing does.

It will take more as it wakes, says Pebble. Limp says. It does not want to. It cannot stop. Unless it is fed.

Fed by what?

By a gardener, says Pebble, and looks at him.

So that is the third cost. The hill that keeps four hundred people alive is being slowly drunk by the thing that might save it, and the only way to stop one from killing the other is to make the garden strong enough to feed itself. It will need herbs sold, and stones spent, and a seed grown. It will need years.

He tells his mother. She listens, and does not speak for a long time, and then she says only: "Then we had better be quick."

She walks the rows alone for an hour after that, while he sits with Pebble. When she comes back she has a list, in her head, which she gives him in the flat tones of a woman planning a siege. No one is to enter but the two of them. The Bell is not to be struck without need. The herbs are to be taken a little at a time, in the dark of the moon, and never from the same bed twice. Hu is not to be told, nor Wenyuan, until Mu is dealt with; and then Wenyuan, only, and in a place where nobody else can hear.

"You will hate it," she says. "Keeping it from him. He is a man who has been lied to by everyone he loved, all his life, and trusts you more than any of us."

"I know."

"I want him to be told. Soon. I only want him told by us." She looks at her hands. "I have kept secrets from this clan for twenty years, Jian, small ones, kind ones, and I have never once been sorry. I think I am going to be sorry about this one. I think that is how I will know it was the right size."

* * *

He does it that evening, in the heart of the Orchard, with the Wardens watching.

It is not a decision made in a moment. It is a decision made over the three days since the quarry, in the slow stubborn way that all his decisions are made, with a notebook and a candle and Hu's drawing paper. He has read the half scroll forty times. He has made a copy, in his own small hand, and hidden it. He has taken the original apart in his mind, character by character, to see what it asks.

It asks for a Seed.

It is, in the end, a very simple method. A five-element root is not a tool for a single trick. It is a field. In a normal cultivator, one element dominates and the others lie fallow; in him, all five stand at once, thin and quiet and dim, like five small flames in a wind. The Canon says that this is not weakness. It is an absence of a wall. If a man can draw the elements down, not one at a time, but all together, he can plant them in a single point of the dantian and let them compete, and let the competition become a root.

It will give him a Seed. The Seed will grow. And the Seed will eat.

That is in the text, in the second paragraph, in the cramped impatient hand of the nameless author. The Seed is hungry. For the first season it takes a fifth of all that the body gains. It is a toll, and a fair one. The harvest comes later.

A fifth, thinks Jian. He has done the sum. It is not a ruinous one. It means that for as long as the Seed is a Seed, a fifth of what he takes in from now will go into it, and not into him, and that his advance will be a fifth slower than it would be. A year of cultivation will take fifteen months.

He has no idea what the harvest is. The scroll stops there.

It is a gamble, he thinks. A little one.

But the Orchard air is dense, and his body has been drinking it for three days, and he is a stage short of the one that matters. A seventh-stage youth of nineteen who wishes to break into the eighth is a boy who has been pressing against a wall for a very long time. The Seed does not open the wall. It only makes a place where, if the wall should give, something will be ready to grow.

Overreach, the panel said. Not recommended below Foundation.

I know.

He sits at the edge of the pool, with the green mist curling round his knees, and his mother ten paces off with a knife on her lap, and the amber eye of the gate Warden fixed on him from across the water. Pebble is on his shoulder. Her small cold feet are curled in the cloth of his collar, and her breath is a faint dry flutter against his ear.

Are you ready? she asks.

No.

Good, says Pebble, with satisfaction. People who are ready are people who have not thought.

He laughs, in spite of himself. Then he lays his hands on his knees, and closes his eyes, and lets the five dim lights in his dantian come together.

* * *

It is not like a breakthrough.

He has broken through before, and he knows the shape of it. The last, in the snow in the granary, was a long hard climb up a staircase of ice. Every one of them was pressure. Every one was a wall giving way.

This is something else. It is a stillness, so deep and so soft that for a long moment he cannot tell whether anything is happening at all. The Orchard Qi comes in at every pore, as a tide comes in on a flat beach. It does not rush. It spreads. It settles in his channels like a fine silt, and the five lights lean toward each other, and touch.

Wood is green. Fire is gold. Earth is brown, a soft deep brown like the soil of the beds. Water is a thin silver-blue. Metal is a clean pale white. They touch, and for a moment they are a tangle of colors, a knot of competing hungers. He feels each one pull. He feels each one resist.

Neither fire nor water, the Canon said. The quiet between.

He lets go.

It is the hardest thing he has done in two lives. He has spent every hour since waking in this body holding on. To the counting, the margins, the stillness, the thread. And now, with five hungry elements tearing at his chest, he does nothing. He sits in the middle of the knot, and does not choose.

Quiet, he thinks. The quiet between.

The knot shudders. And in the space where all five meet, in a place no larger than a grain of rice, something small and round and dark settles into the center of his dantian, and goes still.

It is the Seed.

* * *

When he opens his eyes, the Orchard is brighter.

It is not that the light has changed. It is that he can see it. Every mote in the air, every drift of mist, every silver vein across the stone ceiling, each is distinct and clean, as though he has been looking through a pane of thick glass and someone has taken it away. He can feel the whole garden, row on row, each bed with its own thin hum.

The ache is gone from his rib. The ache is gone from everything. He feels light. He feels like a lamp in a draft.

Five short.

He almost laughs again. He is an eighth-stage youth of nineteen, with a seed in his belly and a Warden at his back, and the door to the next level of the thing in his chest is five points of Creation Energy away. It is exactly the sort of arithmetic the interface likes. It is a cruel, tidy, precise little joke.

"Jian."

His mother's voice. He turns his head. She has risen to her feet. Her face is pale in the green light, and her hand has gone to her throat.

"Your eyes," she says.

"What?"

"They are... there is a ring. Round the black. A very thin ring, pale as a thread." She takes a step toward him. "It is gold. It is moving."

He lifts his hand and touches his own face. It feels the same. His skin is warm, and his lashes are damp, and a faint thin trembling is running through him like the last note of a struck gong.

Five elements, he thinks. In a seed, in the dark.

The toll, says the cold part of him, with great gentleness. You have not paid it yet.

And from the roof of the Orchard, from some place very far above, comes a sound like the whole of the great stone vault drawing breath, and the Wardens, all eleven, without a word, turn together and bow.
